xin.title: Incoming word vectors
xin.body:
One vector per word (from the previous layer, or from embedding + position).

📍 Location: App overview › Agent › LLM › Transformer block › Attention › Incoming word vectors
⚙️ No learnable parameters: a fixed program / fixed rule / value computed on the fly
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

Every token in the sentence has its own vector, and attention processes all the words at once.

🌱 Where it starts

Not a parameter; it’s the result of the previous step.

🔧 How training adjusts it

Not adjusted itself.

▶ What it does in use

The raw material for attention.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

Each word keeps its own vector instead of the whole sentence being squashed into one, so every position’s information is preserved intact and later layers can take what they need.

✅ Why this works

All words can enter attention at once and be computed in parallel; each position can also practise “guessing the next word” on its own.

⚠️ Limits / notes: This is a plain-language description of common practice; actual implementations vary by system.

wq.title: Q table (makes query cards)
wq.body:
Turns a word vector into a “query card”: what kind of word am I looking for?

📍 Location: App overview › Agent › LLM › Transformer block › Attention › Q table (makes query cards)
🔥 Has learnable parameters: adjusted in training, read-only in use
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

  • Word vector × Q table = query card Q.
  • For example, the query card of “apples” is roughly asking: “Is there an earlier word that does something to me?” (an analogy; really it’s a list of numbers).

🌱 Where it starts

Random initialization.

🔧 How training adjusts it

Adjusted to learn to ask “useful questions”.

▶ What it does in use

Read-only; computes a query card for each word.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

  • A word needs different features when it is “looking for others” and when it is “being looked for”.
  • A separate Q table translates word vectors specifically into “what I’m looking for”.

✅ Why this works

Training adjusts the Q table so that truly useful words get higher match scores: the gradient rewards ways of asking that “look at the right people”.

⚠️ Limits / notes: “Query card” is only an analogy; the numbers in Q usually have no readable meaning.

wk.title: K table (makes key cards)
wk.body:
Turns a word vector into a “key card”: what kind of word I am, for others to match against.

📍 Location: App overview › Agent › LLM › Transformer block › Attention › K table (makes key cards)
🔥 Has learnable parameters: adjusted in training, read-only in use
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

Each word wears a key card; “eating”, for example, might read “I’m an action, food-related”. The better someone’s query card matches my key card, the higher the score.

🌱 Where it starts

Random initialization.

🔧 How training adjusts it

Adjusted to learn to put on “easy-to-find labels”.

▶ What it does in use

Read-only; computes a key card for each word.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

  • “What I am, and how I’m found” is a different role, so it gets its own K table.
  • If Q and K used the same table, each word’s match with itself would be naturally inflated, and asymmetric relations like “I’m looking for action words, but I myself am a noun” couldn’t be expressed.

✅ Why this works

With Q and K learned separately, the matching can be asymmetric: “apples” paying close attention to “eating” doesn’t mean “eating” pays the same attention to “apples”.

⚠️ Limits / notes: “Key card” is only an analogy.

wv.title: V table (makes value cards)
wv.body:
Turns a word vector into a “value card”: the information I hand over when others attend to me.

📍 Location: App overview › Agent › LLM › Transformer block › Attention › V table (makes value cards)
🔥 Has learnable parameters: adjusted in training, read-only in use
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

  • The key card decides “whether I get looked at”, the value card decides “what I give when looked at”.
  • Two separate cards make the model more flexible: the features used for matching and the information passed on can differ.

🌱 Where it starts

Random initialization.

🔧 How training adjusts it

Adjusted.

▶ What it does in use

Read-only; computes a value card for each word.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

“Whether I get looked at” (K) and “what I hand over when looked at” (V) are different things: the features used for matching aren’t necessarily the information most worth passing on.

✅ Why this works

Each of the three roles has its own table, each trained into the shape that suits its role best, which makes the model more flexible.

⚠️ Limits / notes: This is a plain-language description of common practice; actual implementations vary by system.

q.title: Q query card (computed)
q.body:
Each word’s question: what am I looking for?

📍 Location: App overview › Agent › LLM › Transformer block › Attention › Q query card (computed)
⚙️ No learnable parameters: a fixed program / fixed rule / value computed on the fly
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

A list of numbers compared against the others’ key cards.

🌱 Where it starts

Not a parameter; computed fresh every time = word vector × Q table.

🔧 How training adjusts it

Not adjusted itself (it’s computed); the Q table is what gets adjusted.

▶ What it does in use

Computed on the spot and discarded after use.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

Query cards aren’t stored but computed on the spot: the same word asks different questions in different sentences and layers, depending on its current vector.

✅ Why this works

The same Q table is shared by all words and positions, so the parameter count doesn’t grow with sentence length.

⚠️ Limits / notes: This is a plain-language description of common practice; actual implementations vary by system.

k.title: K key card (computed)
k.body:
Each word’s label: what am I?

📍 Location: App overview › Agent › LLM › Transformer block › Attention › K key card (computed)
⚙️ No learnable parameters: a fixed program / fixed rule / value computed on the fly
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

A list of numbers that later words compare their query cards against.

🌱 Where it starts

Not a parameter; computed on the spot = word vector × K table.

🔧 How training adjusts it

Not adjusted itself; the K table is what gets adjusted.

▶ What it does in use

Computed on the spot. During text generation the K of earlier words is cached and reused so it needn’t be recomputed every step (usually called the KV cache).

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

Also computed on the spot: the label depends on the word’s current vector (which has already absorbed context).

✅ Why this works

Because of masking, earlier words can’t see later ones, so the K of earlier words doesn’t change when a new word is generated and can be cached and reused (the KV cache), saving a great deal of computation.

⚠️ Limits / notes: The cache takes a lot of GPU memory, especially for long texts (see “KV cache” and “Grouped-query attention”).

v.title: V value card (computed)
v.body:
The information each word can provide.

📍 Location: App overview › Agent › LLM › Transformer block › Attention › V value card (computed)
⚙️ No learnable parameters: a fixed program / fixed rule / value computed on the fly
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

When attended to, it is “mixed” into the attender’s new vector in proportion to the attention.

🌱 Where it starts

Not a parameter; computed on the spot = word vector × V table.

🔧 How training adjusts it

Not adjusted itself; the V table is what gets adjusted.

▶ What it does in use

Computed on the spot; also cached (the KV cache).

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

Also computed on the spot: the information handed over depends on the word’s current vector.

✅ Why this works

Like K, it can be cached and reused; the same V table is shared by all positions.

⚠️ Limits / notes: This is a plain-language description of common practice; actual implementations vary by system.

score.title: ① Score
score.body:
Match query cards against key cards to compute match scores.

📍 Location: App overview › Agent › LLM › Transformer block › Attention › ① Score
⚙️ No learnable parameters: a fixed program / fixed rule / value computed on the fly
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

  • Multiply my Q with each word’s K position by position and add up (dot product), then divide by √(card length) so the scores don’t get so large that the proportions afterwards become extreme.
  • The better the match, the higher the score.

🌱 Where it starts

A fixed formula.

🔧 How training adjusts it

No parameters; not adjusted.

▶ What it does in use

Computed on the spot.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

  • We need a number for “how well a query card matches a key card”.
  • The dot product is the simplest: the more aligned, the larger, and one matrix multiplication computes all pairs of words at once.
  • Then divide by √(card length): the longer the card, the larger and more variable the dot product naturally is, and without scaling softmax would become extreme (almost 100% on one word).

✅ Why this works

  • When the proportions are too extreme the gradient approaches 0 (vanishing gradients) and the model stops learning
  • after scaling the scores stay in a suitable range, the proportions don’t go “all in” from the start, and the training signal flows smoothly.
  • The meaning of high or low dot products is, again, given by training: the Q and K tables are tuned so that “words that deserve attention” get higher dot products.

⚠️ Limits / notes: √length comes from a simple statistical estimate (when the numbers are random and independent, the spread of the dot product is about √length), and works very well in practice.

mask.title: ② Mask (look back only)
mask.body:
Only itself and earlier words may be seen; no peeking at later ones.

📍 Location: App overview › Agent › LLM › Transformer block › Attention › ② Mask (look back only)
⚙️ No learnable parameters: a fixed program / fixed rule / value computed on the fly
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

  • When guessing the next word, the later words don’t exist yet.
  • In training the whole sentence is laid out at once, so the “later positions” must be covered (scores set to minus infinity, becoming 0%) — otherwise the model is just copying the answer.

🌱 Where it starts

A fixed rule.

🔧 How training adjusts it

No parameters; but it is crucial in training: with it, every position in a sentence can practise at the same time without cheating.

▶ What it does in use

Masks the same way, keeping conditions identical to training.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

  • The task is guessing the next word, and the answer is right after it.
  • In training the whole sentence is laid out, so allowing a look ahead would mean copying the answer and learning nothing real.
  • Besides, in use the later words don’t exist yet
  • training and use must have the same conditions.

✅ Why this works

  • Once masked, every position in a sentence can serve at the same time as an exercise that “only sees the text before it”, which makes training very efficient
  • the skills learned apply unchanged in use.

⚠️ Limits / notes: This is how “generative” models work; models built for understanding tasks, such as BERT, don’t mask the later words and use a different kind of exercise.

asoft.title: ③ softmax weights
asoft.body:
Turns match scores into attention weights that add up to 100%.

📍 Location: App overview › Agent › LLM › Transformer block › Attention › ③ softmax weights
⚙️ No learnable parameters: a fixed program / fixed rule / value computed on the fly
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

For example, “apples” looks at: I 12%, love 22%, eating 49%, apples itself 17% (example values).

🌱 Where it starts

A fixed formula.

🔧 How training adjusts it

No parameters.

▶ What it does in use

Computed on the spot.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

  • The match scores need to become “shares”: all non-negative with a fixed total of 100%.
  • That way, however many words come before, the mixed result stays in the same range instead of growing with the number of words.

✅ Why this works

  • High scores are amplified and low scores suppressed, so the model can “focus” attention on a few key words
  • and it is differentiable everywhere, so training can smoothly adjust “look at whom a bit more”.

⚠️ Limits / notes: A fixed total of 1 means attention has to be spent even when no word is particularly relevant; research has found models “park” surplus attention on positions like the beginning.

mix.title: ④ Weighted mix
mix.body:
Mixes everyone’s value cards into one new card according to the attention weights.

📍 Location: App overview › Agent › LLM › Transformer block › Attention › ④ Weighted mix
⚙️ No learnable parameters: a fixed program / fixed rule / value computed on the fly
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

“apples” attends 49% to “eating”, so it takes 49% of the value card of “eating”, plus 22% of the value card of “love”… Combined, that’s the information “apples” has gathered from the context.

🌱 Where it starts

A fixed formula (weighted sum).

🔧 How training adjusts it

No parameters.

▶ What it does in use

Computed on the spot.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

The simplest way to gather information is a weighted average of everyone’s value cards by attention share: the more relevant, the bigger the contribution.

✅ Why this works

  • The result is a new piece of information as long as the original vector, which can be added straight back to it (the residual)
  • the whole process is differentiable, so training can tell the V table “what to hand over”.

⚠️ Limits / notes: A weighted average is itself linear; more complex processing relies on the feed-forward network that follows.

heads.title: ⑤ Concat heads
heads.body:
Several attention groups run at once and their results are joined end to end.

📍 Location: App overview › Agent › LLM › Transformer block › Attention › ⑤ Concat heads
⚙️ No learnable parameters: a fixed program / fixed rule / value computed on the fly
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

  • One set of Q/K/V tables can only learn one “way of looking”, so there are many sets (often dozens of heads)
  • each runs ①–④ independently, and the results are joined into one long list.
  • The division of labour between heads emerges naturally in training.

🌱 Where it starts

Concatenation itself is a fixed operation; each head’s own Q/K/V tables are randomly initialized.

🔧 How training adjusts it

Concatenation has no parameters; each head’s Q/K/V tables are adjusted.

▶ What it does in use

Concatenated on the spot.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

One set of Q/K/V can only produce one set of attention shares, but a word often needs to track several relations at once: grammatical pairings, references (who “it” is), neighbouring words… Multi-head = running several sets in parallel, each looking its own way.

✅ Why this works

Each head uses shorter cards, so the total computation is about the same as one big head, yet it can capture several attention patterns at once, and the concatenated information is richer.

⚠️ Limits / notes: “Heads specialize naturally” is an empirical observation: many heads are hard to interpret, and some research finds removing some heads matters little; why and how they specialize is still being researched.

wo.title: ⑥ Output table
wo.body:
Merges the concatenated multi-head results and brings them back to the original length.

📍 Location: App overview › Agent › LLM › Transformer block › Attention › ⑥ Output table
🔥 Has learnable parameters: adjusted in training, read-only in use
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

Here the findings of all heads are “translated” into one language and fused, then handed to residual + normalization.

🌱 Where it starts

Random initialization.

🔧 How training adjusts it

Adjusted.

▶ What it does in use

Read-only; one multiplication.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

  • After concatenation the heads’ findings are just “sitting side by side”
  • a table is needed to mix them and bring them back to the original length so they can be added to the original vector.

✅ Why this works

Here the heads’ information can combine; the output length matches the original vector, which is what makes the residual addition work.

⚠️ Limits / notes: This is a plain-language description of common practice; actual implementations vary by system.
